Lead with what is at stake in one ruling: every one of those cases, before any has reached a jury. The mechanism: the companies argue federal law pre-empts state-law claims, because emissions cross borders and are a matter for Congress and the federal regulator, so state courts cannot hear deception or nuisance suits at all; say which case is before the court, which companies and which plaintiffs, what the justices asked, and when a ruling is due. Accountability: the suits rest on the companies' own internal research about warming, so say what the plaintiffs allege the firms knew and when, as allegation, and give the companies' answer. Who pays if the cases die: the cities and states now funding sea walls, fire and flood costs from public money. Single source. Dateline Washington. US dateline (1 of 3).

stories.label: Flu season could kick off 'incredibly' early -- what scientists are watching
stories.summary: Surveillance data show the share of influenza tests coming back positive is unusually high for early October in parts of the Northern Hemisphere, and scientists are asking whether annual vaccination should start earlier. Lead with the data: which countries, what positivity rate against the usual level for the date, as Nature gives it. The mechanism: flu vaccine protection wanes within months and campaigns are timed for a winter peak, so a season that starts weeks early catches people unvaccinated, while vaccinating too early leaves them less protected at the end; say which strains are circulating (H3N2 and H1N1 are tagged), what mutations researchers are watching and whether this year's vaccine matches them, and what the Southern Hemisphere season showed. State the uncertainty the scientists state: early positivity does not by itself predict a severe season. Who it concerns: the elderly, infants and the health systems that plan vaccine supply months ahead. This is Nature's news reporting, not a paper. No dateline.

stories.label: Lawmakers Introduce Multiple Laws to Curb Flock After 404 Media Coverage
stories.summary: Senators Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the Ban Flock Act on Friday, which would stop federal agencies from using automatic licence-plate readers, one of several bills now aimed at the surveillance company Flock. Lead with what the bill would prohibit and for whom, and list the other bills and where they were filed, as 404 Media gives it. The mechanism for a technical reader: Flock's cameras log every passing plate into a searchable network shared across thousands of police departments, so a local camera becomes a national tracking system that federal agencies, immigration enforcement among them, can query without a warrant; say what the reporting documented about those searches, what the bills would change (federal use, data sharing, retention), and what they leave untouched, since local police contracts are the bulk of the network. Give Flock's response and the bills' realistic prospects in this Congress, as reported. One clause of context: a Texas city demanded $2 million for public records on its Flock usage (covered 10-05). Single-source original reporting. Dateline Washington. US dateline (2 of 3).

stories.label: Licensing costs driving 90 percent of VMware users to explore options: Survey
stories.summary: A survey of 300 organisations worldwide that run VMware finds about 90% are exploring alternatives because of licensing costs since Broadcom bought the company, yet operational complexity keeps most from leaving. Lead with the gap between the two numbers: how many want out against how many have actually migrated, as Ars gives it. The mechanism for a reader who runs infrastructure: Broadcom ended perpetual licences and bundled products into subscriptions, multiplying bills, and a hypervisor sits under everything (networking, storage, backup, staff skills), so the switching cost is the lock-in; say what price rises respondents report, which alternatives they are evaluating, and what the top barriers are. State the survey's interest plainly: it was published by Rimini Street, which sells third-party support to VMware customers and gains from the finding. Give Broadcom's position if Ars has it. Single source. No dateline: a published survey, not a US dateline.

stories.label: ClickFix campaign in Ukraine compromises over 100 websites to spread Lunex malware
stories.summary: Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA, found more than 100 compromised websites serving fake Cloudflare verification pages that trick visitors into infecting their own machines with the Lunex infostealer. Lead with the scale and the trick. The mechanism for a developer: ClickFix needs no exploit; the fake 'verify you are human' page copies a command to the clipboard and tells the visitor to paste it into the Run dialog or a terminal, so the user executes the malware and browser and mail-gateway defences never see a download; say how the sites were compromised, what Lunex steals (credentials, sessions, wallets, as reported), who the targets are and whether CERT-UA attributes the campaign to a state or criminal group, as attribution and not fact. Say what the report advises defenders to do. Thin feed entry, picked because tech is at its floor and no other security report in the feed is full: write only what the fetched page supports. Single source. Dateline Kyiv.
